# What Claude Code is, and isn't

Claude Code is an AI assistant that runs in your terminal — not in a
web browser.  Unlike the web chat at claude.ai, Claude Code has
direct, controlled access to your local filesystem, your installed
software (R, git, quarto, devtools), and your network.  This means
the assistant can do things like edit `R/calibrate_k_treat.R`
in place, run `Rscript -e "devtools::install()"` and watch the output,
render `extreme_subgroups.qmd` and read the resulting HTML for
warnings — all without you copying anything back and forth.

What it is **not**: a magic black box.  Claude Code asks permission
before doing anything that touches your files or runs external
commands.  You stay in control of every consequential step.  It is
also not a replacement for understanding the work — it accelerates
your judgement, it does not substitute for it.

The single biggest mental shift from the web chat is this: in chat,
the assistant gives you code that *you* run; in Claude Code, the
assistant runs the code itself.  That collapses many of the loops
we have been doing manually (you render, you paste the error, I
diagnose, you patch, you re-render) into a single conversational
turn.

---

# One-time setup

## Install Claude Code

Visit [claude.com/claude-code](https://claude.com/claude-code) and
follow the installation instructions for your operating system.  On
macOS this is typically a single command via Homebrew; on Windows
and Linux there are equivalent installers.  After installation you
will have a `claude` command available in your terminal.

Confirm the install:

```bash
claude --version
```

You will be prompted to sign in on first use; this happens in your
browser and authenticates the CLI to your Anthropic account.

## Verify the local toolchain

Claude Code uses whatever is installed on your machine.  For the
`forestsearch` workflow, that means:

```bash
R --version          # R itself (>= 4.4 recommended)
Rscript --version    # the non-interactive R runner
quarto --version     # Quarto for vignettes
git --version        # for branch operations
```

All four should report versions.  If any are missing, install them
through your usual channel (homebrew, apt, the official installers)
before starting a Claude Code session.

Inside R itself you will want `devtools`, `pak`, and the standard
tidyverse — but if these are not installed, Claude Code can install
them for you on demand when needed.

---

# Starting a session

Open a terminal, navigate to your `forestsearch` working tree, and
launch:

```bash
cd ~/path/to/forestsearch
claude
```

You are now in an interactive Claude Code session, and the assistant
already knows it is running inside the `forestsearch` repository.
It can see the directory tree, read any file, and (with permission)
run any command.

The first message you send sets the tone.  A good opener for our
kind of work would be something like:

> *I am working on the forestsearch package, currently on the
> feature/glm-extension branch.  Please confirm the branch and give
> me a brief summary of recent commits and any uncommitted changes.
> I will then describe what I want to do.*

The assistant will run `git status`, `git log -10 --oneline`, and
report back.  You now have shared context.

---

# How turns work in Claude Code

Each turn is structured the same way as our chat conversations:
you describe what you want, the assistant proposes a plan or asks
for clarification, and then it executes — except "execute" here
means running real commands on your machine.

Three things happen at every consequential step:

1. **Plan.** The assistant tells you what it is about to do.
2. **Permission prompt.** Before any file edit or command execution,
   you are asked to approve.  You can approve once, approve always
   for a given pattern (e.g.\ "always allow `Rscript -e ...`"), or
   deny.
3. **Output.** You see the actual command output — stdout, stderr,
   exit code — exactly as you would if you had typed the command
   yourself.

This is the critical difference from the web chat.  In chat, I
write code, you paste it into your terminal, the output stays on
your screen, you paste it back to me.  In Claude Code, all of that
collapses: the assistant writes the command, you approve, the
output is visible to both of us, and the next turn picks up from
the actual state of your machine.

---

# Walk-through: a session like the ones we have done

The rest of this document is anchored to specific turns we have
done together in the web chat.  For each one I show what the
session would look like in Claude Code instead.

## Scenario 1 — Add `calibrate_k_treat()` to the package

This is the work we did in the most recent vignette session.  In
web chat it took multiple turns: I wrote the function, you copied
it to your local file, you tried to render, you hit the
`verbose = FALSE` duplicate-arg bug, you pasted the traceback, I
fixed it, you re-rendered, it worked.

In Claude Code:

**You.**
> I want to add a new package function `calibrate_k_treat()` that
> calibrates `k_treat` to a target AHR via uniroot on
> `generate_aft_dgm_flex()`.  It should mirror the style of
> `calibrate_k_inter()`.  Please draft the function, save it to
> `R/calibrate_k_treat.R`, document with roxygen, and verify by
> sourcing the file and calling it with a small example.

**Assistant** (in one turn):

1. Reads `R/calibrate_k_inter.R` to match style and house conventions
2. Drafts `R/calibrate_k_treat.R`
3. Asks permission to write the file
4. After writing, runs `Rscript -e 'devtools::document()'`
5. Runs a smoke test:
   ```r
   Rscript -e '
     devtools::load_all()
     library(survival); data(gbsg); gbsg$tm <- gbsg$rfstime / 30.4375
     k <- calibrate_k_treat(0.70,
                            base_args = list(data = gbsg,
                                             continuous_vars = c("age","size"),
                                             factor_vars = "meno",
                                             outcome_var = "tm",
                                             event_var = "status",
                                             treatment_var = "hormon",
                                             model = "null",
                                             n_super = 2000, seed = 99,
                                             verbose = FALSE),
                            verbose = TRUE)
     cat(sprintf("calibrated k_treat = %.4f\\n", k))
   '
   ```
6. Sees the `verbose = FALSE` duplicate-arg error in stderr
7. **Diagnoses on the spot**, edits the function to use
   `utils::modifyList()` instead of `c()`
8. Re-runs the smoke test
9. Confirms convergence

What you saw in web chat as four turns becomes one Claude Code
turn.  The `verbose` bug is caught before it ever reaches you.

## Scenario 2 — Render and review the vignette

Web-chat version: you render locally, save the HTML, upload to me,
I extract content with Python regex, comment on what looks wrong,
you patch and re-render.

Claude Code version:

**You.**
> Please render `extreme_subgroups.qmd` and check the resulting HTML
> for any warnings or errors.  Look particularly at the build-dgm
> chunk output and the forest plots in Part IV.

**Assistant.**

1. Runs `quarto render extreme_subgroups.qmd` and watches stderr
2. Reads the resulting HTML directly (file already on disk)
3. Greps for `<div class="cell-output cell-output-stderr">` blocks
4. Reports findings:
   > Two warnings, one error.  Warning 1: data.table shallow-copy
   > in `build-comparison-data`.  Warning 2: ggplot fixed-aspect
   > with explicit fig.height.  Error: ... etc.
5. Proposes fixes

You can also ask the assistant to compare two renders:

> Render extreme_subgroups.qmd with the AHR calibration on, then
> save the HTML as `out_ahr.html`.  Then switch to use_ahr = FALSE
> in the build-dgm chunk, render again, save as `out_marginal.html`,
> and compare the mHR for the ITT row between the two.  Restore the
> original chunk when done.

The assistant edits, renders, edits back, and reads both HTMLs to
extract the relevant table cells.

## Scenario 3 — Diagnose a calibration issue

Web-chat version: you noticed mHR was 0.64 instead of 0.70, you
attached two HTMLs, I extracted table contents via Python and
diagnosed Cox non-collapsibility.

Claude Code version:

**You.**
> I am seeing simulation median HR around 0.64 even though the DGM
> calibration reports overall HR = 0.70.  Diagnose.

**Assistant.**

1. Reads the relevant qmd chunks to understand the calibration target
   and the simulation analysis
2. Runs an exploratory script:
   ```r
   Rscript -e '
     library(forestsearch); library(survival); library(data.table)
     data(gbsg); gbsg$tm <- gbsg$rfstime / 30.4375
     dgm <- generate_aft_dgm_flex(... matching the qmd setup ...)
     cat("overall (marginal Cox):", dgm$hazard_ratios$overall, "\\n")
     cat("AHR:                   ", dgm$hazard_ratios$AHR, "\\n")
     # Simulate a few trials and check the stratified Cox HR
     hrs <- replicate(100, {
       d <- simulate_from_dgm(dgm, n = 700, ...)
       fit <- coxph(Surv(y_sim, event_sim) ~ treat_sim + strata(grade),
                    data = d)
       exp(coef(fit))
     })
     cat("median simulation HR:  ", median(hrs), "\\n")
   '
   ```
3. Reports the three numbers and explains the gap (non-collapsibility)
4. Proposes the fix (`use_ahr = TRUE`)
5. With your permission, edits the qmd and re-renders

The whole diagnostic loop happens without you having to write or
run anything yourself.

## Scenario 4 — Pull a branch from GitHub

If you want to work against a fresh state — say, comparing your
local working tree against `main` after a teammate's push:

**You.**
> Fetch the latest from origin, show me the diff between my current
> feature/glm-extension and origin/main on R/, and summarise what
> changed.

**Assistant.**

```bash
git fetch origin
git diff origin/main..feature/glm-extension -- R/ | head -200
```

Reads the diff, summarises in plain language.  Useful when you
have been deep in a branch and need to remember what is different
from the trunk before merging.

You can also clone a fresh copy elsewhere for safety:

> Clone the repo to `/tmp/forestsearch-clean`, check out
> `feature/glm-extension`, and install the package from there with
> `devtools::install("/tmp/forestsearch-clean")`.  Do not touch my
> current working tree.

## Scenario 5 — Iterate on a styling change

Web-chat version: you note the All Parameters table looks
mis-aligned, I extract the rendered HTML, propose 4 changes,
you confirm, I write code, you copy-paste into qmd, you re-render,
you upload the new HTML, I check.

Claude Code version:

**You.**
> The "All Parameters" table in fsparams_summary.html looks
> mis-aligned.  Please render the current qmd, look at the table,
> and suggest improvements.  Iterate with me until I am happy.

**Assistant.**

1. Renders, reads the HTML, identifies issues
2. Proposes changes, asks which to apply
3. Applies them, re-renders, shows you the relevant table contents
4. You react, the assistant iterates
5. Final HTML is sitting on your disk, embed-resources already on

The render-paste-extract-react loop becomes a tight conversation.

# Useful commands and patterns

## Common turns and how to phrase them

| Goal | Phrasing |
|:---|:---|
| Start oriented | "Confirm the current branch and any uncommitted changes" |
| Add a function | "Add `R/<name>.R` with [signature/behavior] mirroring `<sibling function>`; document and smoke-test" |
| Find a function | "Where is `<function_name>()` defined? Show me its signature and roxygen header" |
| Render a vignette | "Render `<file>.qmd`. Report any warnings or errors" |
| Compare two states | "Render once with `<setting A>`, save HTML, then with `<setting B>`, and compare `<specific output>`" |
| Branch ops | "Show me the diff between this branch and `<other>` for `R/`" |
| Test a hypothesis | "Test whether [hypothesis] by running a small probe script" |
| Clean up | "Stash my uncommitted changes, render the qmd against `main`, then unstash" |

The pattern: state the *goal* and let the assistant choose the
commands.  You do not need to remember exact R or git syntax.

## Permission management

Three levels:

- **Approve once.** Default.  Each command requires a yes.
- **Approve session.** Approves a pattern (e.g.\ all `Rscript -e ...`
  calls) for the rest of this session.  Speeds up tight loops.
- **Approve always.** Persists across sessions.  Reserve for genuinely
  safe operations like `git status` and read-only file viewing.

If something feels suspicious, deny it and ask the assistant to
explain.  You can always fall back to per-command approval.

## Project rules and the CLAUDE.md file

Claude Code reads a file called `CLAUDE.md` at the root of your
working tree, if one exists, and treats its contents as standing
instructions for that project.  This is how you encode the rules
we developed in our chat sessions.  For example:

```markdown
# CLAUDE.md — forestsearch project rules

## Source of truth
- The most recent version uploaded in conversation, or the file at
  the path I explicitly cite, is the source of truth.  Do not
  pre-emptively re-read from project knowledge unless I ask.
- Always state which version you are building on before any edit.

## Scope discipline
- Modify only what is explicitly requested.  No opportunistic fixes
  or cleanups while doing other work.  Flag side-issues separately
  instead of silently fixing them.

## Before file revisions
- Read the current contents of any file before editing it.
- After any successful str_replace, re-read before further edits to
  the same file — the previous view is stale.

## Style preferences
- Provide source files for functions under discussion as
  downloadable artifacts.
- When in doubt about a deletion, ask first.

## R / package conventions
- Functions go in `R/<name>.R`, one major function per file.
- Match the roxygen style of existing siblings.
- Use the `base_args` named-list pattern for functions wrapping
  `generate_aft_dgm_flex()`.
```

The assistant honours these on every turn within that project,
without you having to re-state them.  This is the equivalent of
the "Strict Session Rules" we developed in chat — except now they
persist across sessions instead of being re-derived each time.

## Tight feedback loops

The biggest win from Claude Code is in tight iteration loops.  A
typical "tune a table layout" cycle:

```
You: The table is too wide.
A:   *edits gt::tab_options, renders, reads HTML*
     Done. The table now fits in 1100px.  Want me to also reduce
     the font for the numeric columns?
You: Yes, but only for the numerics.
A:   *edits, renders, reads HTML*
     Done. The numeric font is now 12px, others stay at 13.
```

Three turns of conversation, three rendered HTMLs, no copying.

---

# Things to avoid

A few rough edges worth knowing about up front.

**Do not let the assistant run open-ended package installs without
review.** `install.packages(...)` on a long dependency chain can be
slow and occasionally pull in surprising versions.  When the
assistant proposes installing something new, ask why and approve
deliberately.

**Long-running R scripts block the conversation.** If you ask for a
20,000-iteration simulation, the assistant will run it and wait.
Better to run those in a separate terminal yourself, save results
to disk, and then ask the assistant to analyse the saved output.
The assistant is good at "20-second probes for diagnosis," less
good at "overnight simulation runs."

**The assistant can edit files.** Real changes, real diffs, real
consequences.  Commit before any non-trivial session so you can
`git restore` if something goes sideways.  A clean git status at
the start of a session is your safety net.

**Authentication for private repos.** If your `forestsearch` clone
is private or uses a non-default SSH key, make sure git operations
work in your terminal *before* starting the Claude Code session.
The assistant uses your existing git credentials; it does not
manage them.

# A worked example: porting our most recent session

Suppose you want to do what we did last time — add
`calibrate_k_treat()` to the package, switch the vignette to AHR
calibration, fix the data.table warning, and improve the
fsparams_summary tables — but in Claude Code instead of web chat.

A plausible session:

```
$ cd ~/forestsearch
$ claude
```

> Confirm branch and recent commits.

(Assistant runs `git status` and `git log -10 --oneline`, reports.)

> Add `R/calibrate_k_treat.R` per the spec we discussed.  Mirror
> `calibrate_k_inter()` style.  Document, install, smoke-test
> against a small GBSG example to confirm convergence on AHR =
> 0.70.

(Assistant drafts, asks permission, writes, runs document + install
+ smoke test.  Reports k_treat value and convergence diagnostic.)

> Now update `extreme_subgroups.qmd` to use the new function.
> Change the calibration to target AHR rather than overall HR.
> Update the prose in Sections 1.4 and 3.3.1 to explain
> non-collapsibility.  Render when done and check the mHR for the
> ITT row matches 0.70.

(Assistant edits, renders, reads HTML, reports ITT mHR.)

> Good.  Now look at fsparams_summary.qmd.  The "All Parameters"
> table is mis-aligned.  Suggest improvements, apply the best two.

(Assistant renders, inspects, proposes changes, applies, re-renders.)

> Commit everything with a sensible message.

(Assistant proposes a commit message, asks permission, commits.)

What took a week of chat turns becomes an afternoon.  The cost is
that you give up some of the explicit "let me see this code before
you run it" review that chat enforces by default.  The permission
prompts replace that review — but they are less thorough than
hand-pasting code into your terminal.

For high-stakes changes (e.g.\ touching exported package
functions), I recommend a blended workflow: discuss the design in
web chat with full review, then implement and verify in Claude
Code with tight loops.  That preserves the strengths of both
modes.

---

# A short troubleshooting list

| Symptom | Likely fix |
|:---|:---|
| `claude: command not found` after install | Restart your shell, or `source ~/.zshrc`/`~/.bashrc` |
| Assistant cannot see a file | Check that you launched `claude` from the right directory |
| Rscript hangs on installation | Cancel, install the package manually with `pak::pak(...)`, restart session |
| Render works in terminal but fails in Claude Code | Usually a working-directory issue; ask the assistant to `getwd()` and confirm |
| Git operations fail | Check your terminal git credentials first; the assistant does not manage them |
| Assistant gets stuck on a long task | Cancel with Ctrl-C; ask it to do the same task in smaller pieces |

# Further reading

- [claude.com/claude-code](https://claude.com/claude-code) — official
  documentation, installation, and updates
- The CLAUDE.md convention is documented in the official docs;
  copy and adapt the example above to your project
- For very long-running or batch workflows, consider combining
  Claude Code with separate background processes you manage in
  another terminal — Claude Code is most powerful in the
  interactive feedback loop, not for unattended runs
